ocar.opportunity: Brain-wide monosynaptic maps onto genetically defined cell classes would show how mouse visual areas, layers, and cell types share and specialize their inputs, beyond pairwise tracing of a few pathways.
ocar.challenge: Single-cell EM connectomics is still out of reach for whole mammalian brains, and rabies tracing can leak, miss synapse types, or create extra starter cells if helper virus travels retrogradely.
ocar.action: Yao, Wang, Hirokawa, Zeng and colleagues, in Nature Neuroscience (2023), present an optimized EnvA-pseudotyped CVS N2c rabies pipeline with TVA66T helper virus, then map brain-wide inputs onto genetically defined populations in mouse visual cortex.
ocar.resolution: They report quantitative target-, layer-, and cell-class-specific presynaptic connectomes, retrograde evidence for dorsal and ventral visual streams, continuously varying subnetworks through higher visual areas, a hierarchy readable from upper- versus lower-layer feedforward and feedback, and a role for layer 6 in reciprocal interhemispheric connections.
ocar.future_work: The authors say novel connections need independent verification, that rabies tropism and glycoprotein dose may bias which synapses are seen, and that their CCFv3 informatics yields fractional input patterns rather than true cell counts per structure.

summaries.beginner: This team uses a carefully tuned rabies virus to list the cells that talk to chosen neuron types in mouse visual cortex across the whole brain. Different visual areas, layers, and cell classes turn out to have distinct input maps, including a two-stream layout and a special role for layer 6 in linking the two hemispheres.
summaries.intermediate: Published in Nature Neuroscience (2023; catalog year 2021), Yao and colleagues describe a scalable monosynaptic rabies pipeline applied as an exemplar to mouse visual cortex. Retrograde input fractions, registered to CCFv3, differ by target area, layer, and cell class and are interpreted as dorsal/ventral streams plus continuously varying higher-area subnetworks. Intracortical hierarchy is derived from upper-layer feedforward versus lower-layer feedback pathways, and layer 6 is implicated in reciprocal interhemispheric connectivity. The discussion flags TVA leak, rare AAV1 retrograde helper spread, incomplete tropism even with CVS N2c, and the choice to compare fractions of total input rather than starter-normalized cell counts.
summaries.advanced: The catalog lists bioRxiv; the extract is the Nature Neuroscience author manuscript (26:350–364). Input comparisons are fractional whole-brain signals after a global background threshold, not per-structure cell counts; the authors note that this can overestimate major sources when total labeled input is small. Novel long-range edges should not be treated as proven without orthogonal mapping. Cre-driver expression, helper titer, and RG level all limit trans-synaptic efficiency. Catalog stages include proofreading, but the work is viral tracing plus informatics, not EM proofreading.

plain_language_summary: This team uses a carefully tuned rabies virus to list the cells that talk to chosen neuron types in mouse visual cortex across the whole brain. Different visual areas, layers, and cell classes turn out to have distinct input maps, including a two-stream layout and a special role for layer 6 in linking the two hemispheres.

ocar.opportunity: Unmyelinated axons dominate many nerves yet are usually skipped in quantitative connectomics because counting them by hand does not scale, biasing projectome descriptions of health and disease.
ocar.challenge: Transmission-EM cross sections of peripheral nerve mix tightly packed unmyelinated fibers of many sizes, so instance segmentation is hard and expert tracing is slow.
ocar.action: Plebani, Biscola, Havton, Dundar and colleagues, in Scientific Reports (2022), train a deep instance-segmentation network on fully annotated TEM images of rat vagus and pelvic nerves and test it both stand-alone and with an expert in the loop.
ocar.resolution: Stand-alone instance-level F1 scores fall between 0.7 and 0.9 on various test images; in the hybrid setting expert annotation labor is reduced by 80%. The authors present the pipeline as a prototype for high-throughput unmyelinated-fiber characterization.
ocar.future_work: They plan nested U-Nets for arbitrary fiber shapes, non-parametric Bayesian open-set instance segmentation, extension to primate and human vagus, myelinated fibers and Schwann cells, resolution-aware augmentation, and models that use spatial arrangement of axons.

summaries.beginner: Most nerve fibers lack myelin and are too numerous to count by hand on electron-microscope pictures. This team trains a computer to outline those fibers in rat nerves and reports that experts spend far less time when the computer drafts first.
summaries.intermediate: Published in Scientific Reports (2022; catalog year 2021), Plebani and colleagues introduce a prototype deep-learning pipeline for instance segmentation of unmyelinated axons in TEM of rat vagus and pelvic nerves, with every axon in the training images individually annotated. They compare training strategies and evaluate stand-alone versus expert-in-the-loop use. Reported stand-alone instance F1 is between 0.7 and 0.9 across test images, with an 80% reduction in expert labor in the hybrid setting. Code is on GitHub (Banus/umf_unet); SPARC portal data are cited under CC-BY.
summaries.advanced: F1 is given as a range across test images, not a single pooled score, and hybrid labor savings are described as preliminary. The work is 2D nerve cross-sections, not volumetric CNS connectomics. Motta et al. cortical reconstructions are cited as the slow, non-high-throughput alternative rather than as a baseline on the same images. Generalization beyond rat vagus/pelvic TEM is proposed, not shown. Catalog method is TEM; organism is unlabeled in metadata.

plain_language_summary: Most nerve fibers lack myelin and are too numerous to count by hand on electron-microscope pictures. This team trains a computer to outline those fibers in rat nerves and reports that experts spend far less time when the computer drafts first.

ocar.opportunity: Serial EM volumes now capture enough of a neuron to study many spine and shaft synapses together, but segmentation still does not scale to the terabyte volumes needed for population synapse biology.
ocar.challenge: Even modern machine-learning segmenters are slow and expensive on large volumes, so synapse-morphology studies remain stuck on small fields of view.
ocar.action: Wildenberg, Li, Badalamente, Uram, Ferrier, and Kasthuri, on bioRxiv (2021), run state-of-the-art flood-filling segmentation of a 0.6 terabyte mouse EM volume on a substantial fraction of Argonne’s 11.69 petaFLOPs Theta machine, with an iterative human–machine loop, then algorithmically extract dendritic spines.
ocar.resolution: They present a petascale workflow intended to make connectomic segmentation routine enough for comparing synapse biology across conditions, and they demonstrate spine extraction from the resulting meshes for morphology analysis. Data are stated as freely available upon request.
ocar.future_work: They argue for cloud-accessible segmentations (e.g. Neurodata) so labs need not store terabyte volumes locally, and they expect more compute-intensive algorithms on leadership machines to improve both turnaround and accuracy.

summaries.beginner: Electron-microscope stacks of brain tissue are huge, so computers that trace cells usually cannot keep up. This group runs those tracing programs on a supercomputer, then automatically pulls out dendritic spines so thousands of synapses can be measured together.
summaries.intermediate: Posted on bioRxiv (2021), Wildenberg and colleagues describe leadership-scale segmentation of a 0.6 TB serial-EM mouse dataset on Theta (11.69 petaFLOPs) at Argonne. Flood-filling networks are trained with human-in-the-loop ground truth; Li developed distributed segmentation and 3D mesh generation on ThetaGPU, with multithreaded experiments on ThetaKNL. They then extract dendritic spines from the segmentation for morphological analysis. The preprint frames petascale compute as a way to make synapse-level EM a more routine method across biological conditions.
summaries.advanced: The selected extract’s discussion is largely acknowledgements and data-availability language; numeric accuracy, spine counts, and wall-clock times are not given in the usable text. Dataset size is 0.6 TB as stated; organism is mouse from keywords and methods, not a named cortical area in the excerpt. Segmentation uses FFN-style methods rather than a newly invented architecture. Catalog stages include infrastructure; this is a compute-scaling paper, not a new connectome release.

plain_language_summary: Electron-microscope stacks of brain tissue are huge, so computers that trace cells usually cannot keep up. This group runs those tracing programs on a supercomputer, then automatically pulls out dendritic spines so thousands of synapses can be measured together.

ocar.opportunity: Cortical computation depends on stereotyped synapses onto the right cell types and the right subcellular domains; knowing how that selectivity is built would also illuminate neurodevelopmental disorders.
ocar.challenge: Much of the targeting literature comes from laminated circuits where cell-type choice is mixed with layer choice, whereas neocortex intermingles many cell types in the same layer.
ocar.action: Gutman-Wei and Brown, in Frontiers in Neural Circuits (2021), review mechanisms of cell-type- and domain-selective synapse formation in developing neocortex: axonal/dendritic guidance, fine-scale morphogenesis, lineage, activity, and transmembrane or secreted molecules.
ocar.resolution: They organize what is known about intracortical target selection, stress that laminar specificity is an inadequate proxy for cell-type bias in cortex, and point to emerging unbiased molecular tools (projection barcoding, growth-cone profiling, APEX/BioID) as ways forward.
ocar.future_work: They flag temporally precise manipulations, understudied roles of glia in cortical target choice, and the likelihood that more targeting molecules will map onto epilepsy, schizophrenia, and intellectual disability.

summaries.beginner: Brain cells in the cortex must wire to particular partners and even to particular parts of those partners, but how they choose is still poorly understood. This review gathers the developmental rules that might explain that choice and notes that cortex is especially hard because many cell types sit mixed together.
summaries.intermediate: Published in Frontiers in Neural Circuits (2021), Gutman-Wei and Brown review how developing neocortical circuits achieve cell-type-biased and subcellular-domain-selective synapses. They contrast laminated systems, where targeting can be confounded with layer, with cortex, where cell bodies and processes of many types intermingle. Mechanisms surveyed include guidance and morphogenesis, lineage, activity dependence, and intercellular molecules, several of which are already linked to neurodevelopmental disorders. They close by highlighting gaps—glial contributions, temporal sequence of events—and new profiling methods for candidate molecules.
summaries.advanced: This is a narrative review, not a new connectome or perturbation dataset; no quantitative targeting fractions appear in the extract. Claims about disorder genes (L1CAM, ERBB4, FGF13) are cited associations, not results of this paper. Catalog dimension is cell-types; the review is developmental synaptic specificity rather than EM reconstruction.

plain_language_summary: Brain cells in the cortex must wire to particular partners and even to particular parts of those partners, but how they choose is still poorly understood. This review gathers the developmental rules that might explain that choice and notes that cortex is especially hard because many cell types sit mixed together.

ocar.opportunity: Complete larval and adult fly connectomes now make it possible to watch how a whole circuit rewires when one cell type is moved or removed, rather than studying pairs of neurons in isolation.
ocar.challenge: Spatial targeting, molecular partner recognition, and activity all shape synapses, and it has been hard to separate first-order changes in manipulated cells from second- and third-order changes in partners and neighbors.
ocar.action: Donà and Jefferis, in a Current Biology (2021) dispatch, highlight Valdes-Aleman and colleagues’ synaptic-resolution perturbations of a Drosophila larva mechanosensory circuit as a template for comparative connectomics of assembly.
ocar.resolution: They argue that scoring global rewiring—manipulated neurons, their partners, and neighbors—offers a path to principles of wiring specificity, contrasting fly partner-following with mouse sensory–motor arcs that do not fully redirect.
ocar.future_work: They sketch combining whole-brain EM outcomes with molecular data to reverse-engineer developmental programs, noting that most specificity studies still address pairs rather than circuit-wide effects.

summaries.beginner: A commentary explains a fly-larva study that changed one cell type and then remapped the circuit at synapse resolution. The lesson is that comparing wiring diagrams after a developmental tweak can reveal which rules actually build specific connections.
summaries.intermediate: In Current Biology (2021), Donà and Jefferis discuss Valdes-Aleman et al. on single-cell-type perturbations of a larval Drosophila mechanosensory circuit. They place the work in a connectomics expansion from C. elegans to larval and adult fly brains, and they emphasize first-, second-, and third-order rewiring as a way to weigh partner identity versus spatial cues. Contrasts include olfactory receptor neurons that follow displaced partners versus mouse reflex-arc neurons that do not fully redirect, plus a possible anatomy–function mismatch implying compensation. The dispatch is advocacy for comparative developmental connectomics, not a new volume.
summaries.advanced: This is a journal dispatch, not primary data. Mechanistic claims belong to Valdes-Aleman et al. (cited as reference 5) and other cited work (Arber et al. on mouse). No synapse counts or genotype lists appear in the extract. Catalog organism is fly; the piece also discusses worm and mouse examples by way of contrast.

plain_language_summary: A commentary explains a fly-larva study that changed one cell type and then remapped the circuit at synapse resolution. The lesson is that comparing wiring diagrams after a developmental tweak can reveal which rules actually build specific connections.

ocar.opportunity: Segmenting neuronal nuclei in large 3D volumes would let cell-lineage and expression studies move beyond tiny cubes that cannot represent whole brain regions.
ocar.challenge: Existing neuronal-nuclei datasets are usually smaller than 10^{-3} mm^3 with fewer than 500 instances, hiding diversity of appearance and density at sub-cubic-millimeter scale.
ocar.action: Lin, Wei, Petkova, Lichtman, Pfister and colleagues introduce the NucMM dataset at MICCAI (2021): two fully annotated volumes—one 0.1 mm^3 EM volume of nearly an entire zebrafish brain (~170,000 nuclei) and one 0.25 mm^3 micro-CT volume of mouse visual cortex (~7,000 nuclei)—plus a hybrid-representation learning model combining foreground mask, contour map, and signed distance transform.
ocar.resolution: They report great diversity of nuclear appearance and density across the two modalities and volume sizes, quantify those challenges statistically, and find that the hybrid model significantly outperforms state-of-the-art nuclei segmentation methods on NucMM benchmarks.
ocar.future_work: Code and data are released at the project site; how well the hybrid representation transfers outside these two volumes is left to later use of the benchmark.

summaries.beginner: Counting cell nuclei in three-dimensional brain images gets harder as the chunk of tissue gets bigger. This paper releases two large labeled volumes—one fish brain in electron microscopy and one piece of mouse cortex in micro-CT—and a computer method that outlines nuclei more accurately than earlier tools on those data.
summaries.intermediate: Presented at MICCAI (2021), Lin and colleagues curate NucMM: a 0.1 mm^3 EM volume covering nearly the entire zebrafish brain with about 170,000 nuclei, and a 0.25 mm^3 micro-CT volume of part of mouse visual cortex with about 7,000 nuclei. They argue prior nuclei datasets were too small (<10^{-3} mm^3, <500 instances) to capture appearance and density diversity. A hybrid model that fuses foreground, contour, and signed-distance representations is reported to beat contemporary nuclei segmenters on this benchmark, with code and data at connectomics-bazaar.github.io/proj/nucMM.
summaries.advanced: The attached PDF extract is a different paper (Qureshi and Reis on functional graphs of power maps over finite groups); this annotation follows the catalog abstract only. Instance counts (~170,000; ~7,000) and volume sizes are abstract figures. “Significantly outperforms” is not accompanied by numeric scores in the usable source. Catalog organisms are mouse and zebrafish; methods include electron microscopy.

plain_language_summary: Counting cell nuclei in three-dimensional brain images gets harder as the chunk of tissue gets bigger. This paper releases two large labeled volumes—one fish brain in electron microscopy and one piece of mouse cortex in micro-CT—and a computer method that outlines nuclei more accurately than earlier tools on those data.

ocar.opportunity: MRI network science now draws human prefrontal “connectomes,” but those maps need to be checked against the monosynaptic hard wiring known from non-human primate tracing.
ocar.challenge: Imaging edges can be indirect or second-order, so hubs and modules inferred from MRI may not match cells of origin, axon trajectories, and terminals defined anatomically.
ocar.action: Haber, Liu, Seidlitz, and Bullmore, in Neuropsychopharmacology (2022), review region-by-region NHP prefrontal pathways, MRI structural and functional connectivity methods, and graph-theoretic hubs and modules, then align tracing and imaging with concrete PFC examples.
ocar.resolution: They treat anatomic tracing as the ground for interpreting MRI nodes, hubs, and edges, and they argue that highly connected hubs are central both to network integration and to neurodegenerative and neurodevelopmental disorders, while remaining cautious that imaging often does not reflect direct wiring.
ocar.future_work: They call the field back to evaluating how well indirect MRI measurements match NHP tracing, with implications for how circuits interact and for therapeutic interventions such as deep-brain stimulation.

summaries.beginner: Maps of the human prefrontal cortex from MRI may not match the actual one-synapse wiring known from monkey anatomy. This review puts those two kinds of map side by side so imaging hubs can be read more carefully.
summaries.intermediate: Published in Neuropsychopharmacology (2022; catalog year 2021), Haber and colleagues review monosynaptic prefrontal connections in non-human primates and compare them with MRI-derived human networks. They outline anatomic pathways for each PFC region, then survey structural and functional MRI and graph measures of hubs, modules, and integration. Worked examples show how tracing can inform the composition of PFC nodes and the edges linking PFC to cortex and subcortex. The closing argument is that neuroimaging has led on complex topology but must be checked against hard wiring before treating imaged connections as direct.
summaries.advanced: This is a review; no new tracer matrix or MRI cohort is reported in the extract. Hub-disease claims cite the imaging literature rather than a new analysis here. Catalog stages include proofreading, which does not describe this anatomical/imaging synthesis. Species contrast is NHP tracing versus human MRI, not a single matched dataset.

plain_language_summary: Maps of the human prefrontal cortex from MRI may not match the actual one-synapse wiring known from monkey anatomy. This review puts those two kinds of map side by side so imaging hubs can be read more carefully.

ocar.opportunity: Miniature insects keep complex brains with thousands of identifiable, stereotyped neurons at body sizes comparable to unicellular organisms, so they could shrink the cost of complete circuit maps.
ocar.challenge: Standard model brains (macaque, mouse, zebrafish, fly, nematode) are still large or otherwise costly relative to the mapping problem, and invasive human experiments are impractical.
ocar.action: Makarova, Polilov, and Chklovskii, in Current Opinion in Neurobiology (2021), propose adding miniature insects to the neuroscience model-organism set and review why their brains retain insect advantages (identifiability, connectome stereotypy) while being easier to map.
ocar.resolution: They argue that the smallest insect brains offer both a practical path to complete maps and evolutionary insight into compact brain design.
ocar.future_work: The piece is a prospective argument; mapping a named miniature-insect species end-to-end is the implied next step rather than a result reported here.

summaries.beginner: Some insects are almost as small as single cells yet still have brains with thousands of neurons. This opinion piece argues that those tiny brains would be cheaper and faster to map completely than the usual laboratory animals.
summaries.intermediate: In Current Opinion in Neurobiology (2021), Makarova, Polilov, and Chklovskii argue that miniature insects should join macaque, mouse, zebrafish, fly, and nematode as neuroscience models. Despite body sizes comparable to unicellular organisms, these insects retain complex brains with thousands of neurons, plus insect-typical identifiability and connectome stereotypy at smaller absolute scale. The authors present them as a way to reduce cost and speed whole-brain research while also illuminating evolution of compact circuits.
summaries.advanced: The attached PDF extract is a different paper (Wang et al. 2026 Plants review on Trichogramma semiochemicals); this annotation follows the catalog abstract only. No neuron counts for a named miniature species, imaging methods, or reconstruction statistics appear in the usable source. Catalog organism is fly; the essay’s focus is miniature insects more broadly.

plain_language_summary: Some insects are almost as small as single cells yet still have brains with thousands of neurons. This opinion piece argues that those tiny brains would be cheaper and faster to map completely than the usual laboratory animals.

ocar.opportunity: A full Platynereis larva connectome plus a multimodal cellular atlas now let comparative anatomists ask what core circuits the first bilaterian brain may have contained.
ocar.challenge: Extant bilaterian brains are diverse, so relating today’s circuits to an ancestral composite of a circular CNS and an apical sensory-neurosecretory system requires aligned gene-expression and ultrastructure.
ocar.action: Arendt, Quintana Urzainqui, and Vergara, in Current Opinion in Neurobiology (2021), review those landmark Platynereis resources and interpret the young worm’s brain as a composite: anterior circular CNS fused to an apical system, with lhx6-arx-dlx chemosensory circuits seeding later associative centers.
ocar.resolution: They propose this composite as the conserved core of the nereid brain and as a reference for descending bilaterian lineages.
ocar.future_work: How far the lhx6-arx-dlx motif and apical-plus-circular fusion generalize beyond annelids is the comparative question the review sets up.

summaries.beginner: A small marine worm’s young brain has now been mapped in unusual detail. This review uses that map to guess which parts of our distant ancestors’ first brain still show up in animals today.
summaries.intermediate: In Current Opinion in Neurobiology (2021), Arendt, Quintana Urzainqui, and Vergara discuss the Platynereis dumerilii larva as a comparative neuroanatomy model, citing a full connectome and a multimodal cellular atlas that combines gene expression with ultrastructure. They argue the ancestral bilaterian brain was composite: the anterior end of a circular CNS fused to a sensory-neurosecretory apical system. Chemosensory lhx6-arx-dlx neurons are proposed as a source of associative centers in later lineages.
summaries.advanced: The attached PDF extract is a different paper (Verasztó, Jasek, Jékely et al., eLife 2024, whole-body connectome of a segmented annelid larva); this annotation follows the catalog abstract only. Cell-type counts, synapse numbers, and module lists from that eLife reconstruction were not used. The CONB piece is interpretive comparative anatomy, not a methods paper. Catalog organism is “other”; method metadata lists acquisition.

plain_language_summary: A small marine worm’s young brain has now been mapped in unusual detail. This review uses that map to guess which parts of our distant ancestors’ first brain still show up in animals today.

ocar.opportunity: Mammalian circuits span synapses to whole brains, so a single preparation that can be imaged with light and then electron microscopy would let targeted long-range axons be followed to identified synapses.
ocar.challenge: Volume EM still covers only tens to hundreds of micrometers, while fluorescence can track projections brain-wide but not resolve synaptic ultrastructure in the same volume without destroying it.
ocar.action: Furuta, Yamauchi, Hioki and colleagues, on bioRxiv (2021), couple successive LM/EM imaging to ScaleSF, an ultrastructure-preserving clearing method, and apply the pipeline to mouse striatofugal, mouse callosal, and marmoset corticostriatal systems with EGFP-APEX2 labeling.
ocar.resolution: They demonstrate macroscopic, mesoscopic, microscopic, and EM views of the same labeled axons, including TEM of targeted synapses and FIB-SEM of a mouse callosal input onto a PV interneuron, arguing for targeted interrogation of circuit structure and synaptic connectivity together.
ocar.future_work: The preprint presents the method as a way to expand the spatial scales of objects in brain-wide connectivity studies; how far ScaleSF plus APEX2 generalizes beyond the three demonstrated projections is left open.

summaries.beginner: Brain wiring has to be seen both as a whole-brain sketch and as tiny synapses. This team clears tissue in a way that still works for electron microscopy, so they can zoom from a whole slice down to a chosen synapse in mouse and marmoset.
summaries.intermediate: Posted on bioRxiv (2021), Furuta, Yamauchi, Hioki and colleagues introduce multi-scale LM/EM imaging with ScaleSF clearing. The workflow runs from brain-wide observation through mesoscopic mapping and subcellular light microscopy to EM of nanoscopic structures. They apply it to mouse striatofugal axons, mouse callosal axons (including inputs onto PV interneurons with FIB-SEM of PSDs), and marmoset corticostriatal projections using AAV SynTetOff EGFP-APEX2 (and a FLEX-mScarlet partner for PV). Figure examples show correlated CLSM, DAB-Ni2+ APEX2 labeling, and TEM of identified synapses.
summaries.advanced: The selected extract’s later pages are figure legends rather than a limitations section; quantitative clearing metrics, synapse counts, and success rates are not in the usable text. Catalog organism is mouse, but a marmoset corticostriatal example is also demonstrated. This is correlative targeted EM, not a dense connectome. Clearing is ScaleSF specifically, claimed to preserve ultrastructure.

plain_language_summary: Brain wiring has to be seen both as a whole-brain sketch and as tiny synapses. This team clears tissue in a way that still works for electron microscopy, so they can zoom from a whole slice down to a chosen synapse in mouse and marmoset.

ocar.opportunity: Combining neuroimaging with genetically informative designs can show how DNA variation and gene expression shape the human structural and functional connectome.
ocar.challenge: Heritability, specific variants, and spatial coupling to transcription are different questions, each with distinct strengths and biases, and genetic effects are not uniform across the brain.
ocar.action: Arnatkevičiūtė, Fulcher, Bellgrove, and Fornito, in NeuroImage (2021), review three frameworks: twin-based heritability, association studies linking DNA variants to imaging phenotypes, and correlations between imaging maps and transcriptional atlases.
ocar.resolution: They report converging evidence that anatomical connectivity is under stronger genetic influence than functional connectivity, and that genetic control is regionally heterogeneous. They also discuss how imaging genetics can inform brain dysfunction in clinical disorders.
ocar.future_work: The review treats integration of the three frameworks, and extension to disorder mechanisms, as ongoing rather than solved.

summaries.beginner: This review asks how genes help build the wiring and activity patterns of the human brain. It compares family studies, DNA-variant studies, and maps of gene activity in brain tissue, and it reports that physical wiring looks more heritable than functional coupling.
summaries.intermediate: Published in NeuroImage (2021; catalog DOI is an OSF preprint), Arnatkevičiūtė and colleagues review genetic bases of human brain networks via twin heritability, variant-association studies, and imaging–transcription spatial correlations. They summarize foundations, strengths, limitations, and discoveries of each approach. Converging evidence is that anatomical connectivity is under stronger genetic influence than functional connectivity, with uneven regional and connectional genetic control. Clinical translation is discussed as a use case rather than a new cohort analysis.
summaries.advanced: The attached PDF extract is a different paper (Sipes, Nagarajan, and Raj, bioRxiv 2026, gene gradients and directed structural connectivity); this annotation follows the catalog abstract only. No heritability coefficients or named loci from the NeuroImage review appear in the usable source. Catalog journal is NeuroImage; uuid is the OSF preprint DOI.

plain_language_summary: This review asks how genes help build the wiring and activity patterns of the human brain. It compares family studies, DNA-variant studies, and maps of gene activity in brain tissue, and it reports that physical wiring looks more heritable than functional coupling.

ocar.opportunity: If synaptic graphs of diseased tissue can be mapped as carefully as healthy connectomes, rewiring rules might point to therapeutic targets rather than only to cell loss.
ocar.challenge: Neurodegeneration is not a static cut of neuron A from C; added neurons and synapses, plus sprouting, rapidly complicate the graph, and early retinal remodeling is hard to see without ultrastructure.
ocar.action: Pfeiffer, Anderson, Marc, Jones and colleagues, on bioRxiv (2020), build RPC1, an open-access ssTEM pathoconnectome from a rabbit model of autosomal-dominant cone-sparing retinitis pigmentosa, and annotate rod-pathway topology.
ocar.resolution: They report aberrant rod-network connectivity and novel synapses from neurite sprouting, including gap-junctional coupling between rod bipolar cells and Aii amacrine cells before rods are fully gone, compromising spatial and temporal resolution of the intact network.
ocar.future_work: Later-stage pathoconnectomes are proposed to track when networks fail and where interventions might act; they argue retinal remodeling shares components with CNS negative plasticity and proteomic findings in Alzheimer’s and Parkinson’s disease.

summaries.beginner: When photoreceptors die, the remaining retinal circuit does not simply go quiet—it rewires. This team maps those new and broken connections in a rabbit model of retinitis pigmentosa at electron-microscope resolution.
summaries.intermediate: Posted on bioRxiv (2020), Pfeiffer and colleagues introduce pathoconnectomics with RPC1, an ssTEM volume from a rabbit model of autosomal-dominant cone-sparing retinitis pigmentosa, building on their earlier healthy retinal connectome RC1. They observe early breakdown of primary visual pathways, including gap junctions between rod bipolar cells and Aii amacrine cells prior to complete rod loss, plus novel synapses from neurite sprouting. Viking annotation and computational molecular phenotyping are used to assemble the volume. The authors present this as a map for therapeutics and as a model of neurodegenerative rewiring beyond the retina.
summaries.advanced: Catalog organism is mouse; the extract is a rabbit RP model. “First pathoconnectome” is an authorship claim. Quantitative synapse counts and animal numbers are not in the selected text. Gap-junction RodBC–Aii coupling is the highlighted early motif; generalization to Alzheimer’s/Parkinson’s is analogical (remodeling components and proteomics), not a demonstration in those tissues. Preprint, not the later journal version, is the extract source.

plain_language_summary: When photoreceptors die, the remaining retinal circuit does not simply go quiet—it rewires. This team maps those new and broken connections in a rabbit model of retinitis pigmentosa at electron-microscope resolution.

ocar.opportunity: C. elegans remains the only metazoan long mapped at the level of genes, cells, and synapses together, so it can still teach how a nervous system is built from lineage to connectivity.
ocar.challenge: Modern work on glia, sexual dimorphism, and developmental plasticity can look disconnected from Brenner and Sulston unless those threads are pulled back to the original maps.
ocar.action: Rapti, in Journal of Neurogenetics (2020), offers a perspective on C. elegans neurodevelopment from early visionaries through current research, summarizing generation and diversification of neural components, navigation, and connectivity.
ocar.resolution: The essay highlights glia biology, sex dimorphism, and plasticity, and argues that connecting genes to cell function and behavior in this system still yields mechanistic questions for future work.
ocar.future_work: Emerging questions are framed rather than experimentally closed; the piece is a historical and conceptual survey.

summaries.beginner: The roundworm C. elegans was the first animal with a complete cell lineage, genome, and wiring diagram. This perspective retells how that toolkit still drives discoveries about how nervous systems develop.
summaries.intermediate: In Journal of Neurogenetics (2020), Rapti surveys C. elegans neurodevelopment from Brenner, Sulston, and colleagues through a growing neuroscience community. The worm is described as the first metazoan with a complete cell lineage, sequenced genome, and connectome. Topics include generation and diversification of neural components, axon navigation, connectivity, and newer emphases on glia, sexual dimorphism, and developmental plasticity. The stance is that multifaceted model-organism work still converts gene–cell–behavior links into open mechanistic questions.
summaries.advanced: The attached PDF extract is a different paper (Yu et al., Scientific Reports, particle-filter tracking of colliding C. elegans); this annotation follows the catalog abstract only. No new synapse counts or lineage statistics appear in the usable source. Catalog organism is elegans; the piece is a perspective, not a methods paper.

plain_language_summary: The roundworm C. elegans was the first animal with a complete cell lineage, genome, and wiring diagram. This perspective retells how that toolkit still drives discoveries about how nervous systems develop.

ocar.opportunity: Larval and adult Drosophila now have cell-type, connectome, and synaptome resources that could be executed as models rather than left as separate tables.
ocar.challenge: Those resources live in disparate databases, and exploring 3D anatomy is still weakly coupled to running circuits and comparing models across labs, stages, and datasets.
ocar.action: Lazar, Liu, Turkcan, and Zhou, on bioRxiv (2020), introduce FlyBrainLab: an open-source interactive environment that binds neuroanatomy, genetics, and physiology to executable circuits, with utility libraries for graphs and circuit libraries for central complex and early olfaction.
ocar.resolution: The platform supports 3D exploration, launching models from visualized data, cross-model comparison, and extra libraries for visual and olfactory molecular transduction so sensory activity can help validate executable circuits.
ocar.future_work: The authors position FlyBrainLab as infrastructure for discovering functional logic beyond the static connectome; uptake and biological validation of user-built circuits are the implied test.

summaries.beginner: Fly brains now come with rich wiring and cell-type catalogs that are hard to use together. FlyBrainLab is a software workbench that lets researchers look at those maps in 3D and immediately run them as living circuit models.
summaries.intermediate: Posted on bioRxiv (2020), Lazar, Liu, Turkcan, and Zhou present FlyBrainLab as an interactive open-source computing environment for Drosophila. It integrates computational models with neuroanatomical, neurogenetic, and electrophysiological data and supports comparison across researchers, developmental stages, and datasets. Utility libraries extract graphs from raw connectome/synaptome data; circuit libraries target central-complex neuropils and adult and larval early olfactory systems. Additional libraries cover molecular transduction in vision and olfaction as entry points for sensory circuit function and in-platform biological validation.
summaries.advanced: The selected extract’s later pages are references, not a limitations section; no runtime benchmarks or user-study metrics appear. “Uniquely positioned” is an authorship claim. Catalog stages include infrastructure, graph_analysis, and modeling, which match the software’s stated scope. This is a platform paper, not a new EM volume.

plain_language_summary: Fly brains now come with rich wiring and cell-type catalogs that are hard to use together. FlyBrainLab is a software workbench that lets researchers look at those maps in 3D and immediately run them as living circuit models.

ocar.opportunity: C. elegans connectomes catalog many gap junctions, and 25 innexin genes are expressed in shifting spatial and temporal patterns, so electrical synapses can be studied genetically in a complete wiring diagram.
ocar.challenge: Innexins act as channels and hemichannels, can be heteromeric, and change under stress (e.g. dauer), so their developmental and circuit roles are easy to undersell if they are treated only as static bidirectional pores.
ocar.action: Jin, Park, Lyu, and Jin, in Biology Open (2020), review historical and recent findings on gap junctions and innexins in the worm nervous system, including dauer-specific INX-6 coupling of AIB to BAG.
ocar.resolution: They highlight diverse roles in circuit formation and function in both normal and stressful conditions, using dauer locomotion defects of inx-6 or inx-4/che-7 and ectopic inx-6 in non-dauers as a worked example.
ocar.future_work: Open issues include channel composition for most innexins, how gap junctions turn over relative to chemical synapses, and how innexins act downstream of stress-regulated transcription.

summaries.beginner: Worms use protein pores called gap junctions to let neighboring cells share signals quickly. This review collects what is known about those pores in C. elegans, including special wiring that appears only when the animal enters a stress-resistant dauer state.
summaries.intermediate: Published in Biology Open (2020), Jin, Park, Lyu, and Yishi Jin review innexin gap junctions in C. elegans. Connectomic reconstructions document abundant electrical synapses; the genome encodes 25 innexins with dynamic expression. A detailed example is dauer-specific inx-6 in AIB neurons forming gap junctions with BAG via INX-6 and INX-4/CHE-7, required for dauer-specific locomotion and sufficient to induce that behavior when inx-6 is expressed ectopically in non-dauers. Transcription factors unc-42 and daf-16 are cited as required for inx-6 upregulation. The review argues these findings inform gap junctions in all animals.
summaries.advanced: This is a review; EM dauer connectivity is attributed to Bhattacharya et al. (2019) and others, not newly quantified here. Most innexin channel stoichiometries remain unknown, as the authors note. Catalog dimension is connectomics; the piece is molecular/circuit review rather than a new volume. Molecules below ~1 kDa is the cited permeation scale from Goodenough.

plain_language_summary: Worms use protein pores called gap junctions to let neighboring cells share signals quickly. This review collects what is known about those pores in C. elegans, including special wiring that appears only when the animal enters a stress-resistant dauer state.

ocar.opportunity: An open marmoset retrograde/anterograde tracing repository makes it possible to chart mesoscale cortico-cortical topology in a primate increasingly used for applied neuroscience.
ocar.challenge: Whether that network shows the same segregation–integration motifs reported in other species, scales, and reconstruction methods was untested for this connectome.
ocar.action: Liu, Zheng, and Mišić, in Network Neuroscience (2020), analyze the Marmoset Brain Architecture Project cortico-cortical matrix for path length, multiscale communities, a connective core, motif composition, and topological cavities.
ocar.resolution: They find near-minimal path length, nested specialized communities, hubs forming a densely interlinked core (often in polysensory association cortex), a distinctive motif fingerprint, and cavities that can attenuate signaling. They interpret these as a conserved phylogenetic toolkit.
ocar.future_work: They expect the map to ground later anatomical, functional, and behavioral marmoset studies linking unimodal modules to association-core integration.

summaries.beginner: Researchers turned an open map of marmoset cortical wiring into a network sketch. The sketch shows clustered specialist areas plus a tightly linked core that can mix information, a pattern also seen in other animals.
summaries.intermediate: Published in Network Neuroscience (2020), Liu, Zheng, and Mišić chart topology of the mesoscale marmoset cortico-cortical connectome from the Marmoset Brain Architecture Project. Reported non-random features include high clustering with a nested community hierarchy, near-minimal path length via high-degree hubs that are densely interlinked (a connective core), a unique motif composition, and multiple topological cavities. Specialized communities tend to encompass unimodal areas, whereas high-participation rich-club areas sit in polysensory association cortex. The authors argue these attributes balance segregation and integration and match reports across species and scales.
summaries.advanced: This is a graph analysis of an existing tracing repository, not a new tracer study. “Universal across phylogeny” is an interpretive claim from concordance, not a formal phylogenetic test. Numeric clustering coefficients, cavity counts, and hub lists are not in the selected extract. Catalog stages include proofreading, which does not describe this paper; it is mesoscale tract-tracing topology.

plain_language_summary: Researchers turned an open map of marmoset cortical wiring into a network sketch. The sketch shows clustered specialist areas plus a tightly linked core that can mix information, a pattern also seen in other animals.

ocar.opportunity: Microscope throughput is outrunning local analysis, so a modular HPC workflow that can be triggered during acquisition would keep segmentation close to the beam.
ocar.challenge: Community EM tools are developed independently, few labs can run an end-to-end stack, and petabyte volumes will not fit workstations or small clusters.
ocar.action: Vescovi, Li, Kinnison, Kasthuri, Uram, Ferrier and colleagues, at XLOOP (2020), assemble a scalable pipeline that wraps existing EM packages with minimal source changes, orchestrated by a Balsam database, and demonstrate end-to-end segmentation on a supercomputer.
ocar.resolution: A 6700×9900×1312 voxel volume at 12×12×40 nm^3 was split into 3618 overlapping 512×512×128 cubes; FFN inference ran 72 hours on 32 Cooley nodes (2 NVIDIA K80 GPUs each) before workstation reconciliation and Neuroglancer visualization. The pipeline was tested on datasets as large as 1 TB.
ocar.future_work: They are studying larger-scale execution on Argonne machines and note that new modules can target different accelerators; limits are data sharing and allocation size rather than a fixed algorithm ceiling.

summaries.beginner: Electron-microscope movies of brain slices create more data than a desktop can chew. This paper strings together existing tracing programs on a supercomputer so neurons can be reconstructed as the images come in.
summaries.intermediate: Presented at the XLOOP workshop (2020), Vescovi, Li and colleagues describe a modular HPC pipeline from EM images to 3D neuron visualization. Steps were tested on workstation, cluster, and supercomputer; Balsam workflows can start during acquisition. In one demonstration, after U-Net/watershed soma and vessel masking at 4× downsample, a 6700×9900×1312 voxel volume (12×12×40 nm^3) was tiled into 3618 cubes with 32×32×16 overlap; flood-filling inference ran 72 h on 32 Cooley nodes. They report tests up to 1 TB and argue HPC avoids cloud cost for upcoming faster microscopes.
summaries.advanced: The 72-hour Cooley run is one demonstrated volume, not a general throughput SLA. A pre-trained FFN model from Januszewski is acknowledged; novelty is integration and scaling. Catalog journal is the workshop proceedings. “Fully modular and scalable” is the authors’ design claim; larger Argonne runs are promised as future work in the extract.

plain_language_summary: Electron-microscope movies of brain slices create more data than a desktop can chew. This paper strings together existing tracing programs on a supercomputer so neurons can be reconstructed as the images come in.

ocar.opportunity: If physical distance, cytological type, and wiring obey shared rules across mammals, those rules could be extrapolated even to species without complete tracer matrices, including humans.
ocar.challenge: Cortices differ hugely in size, cell composition, and phylogeny, so species-general principles are easy to confuse with species-specific layout, including where the network core sits.
ocar.action: Goulas, Majka, Rosa, and Hilgetag, in PLoS Biology (2019), compare mouse, cat, marmoset, and macaque cortico-cortical connectomes against cytoarchitectonic grades and geometry.
ocar.resolution: Connection existence relates to cytology beyond distance, but that relation is weaker in mouse and marmoset. Laminar origins track cytoarchitectonic gradients rather than the rostrocaudal axis, supporting extrapolation to humans. All four connectomes have a communication core, displaced toward less neuronally dense cortex in cat and macaque.
ocar.future_work: They interpret commonalities and differences as variation on conserved developmental mechanisms; mouse laminar-origin data were not available cortex-wide, so that analysis omitted mouse.

summaries.beginner: Four mammals’ cortical wiring diagrams are compared to see what is shared and what is species-specific. Cell-type architecture, not just distance, helps predict which areas connect, and the most central hubs sit in different kinds of cortex in different species.
summaries.intermediate: Published in PLoS Biology (2019), Goulas and colleagues analyze mouse, cat, marmoset, and macaque cortical connectomes. Mouse analyses use a 48×48 matrix as the logical AND of anterograde and retrograde tracers (plus a 33×33 combined matrix). Connection probability relates to cytoarchitectonic type in addition to distance, attenuated in mouse and marmoset. Laminar origin of connections follows cytoarchitectonic gradients rather than the rostrocaudal axis. A network core is present in all species but shifts toward less neuronally dense cortex in cat and macaque, with possible functional and vulnerability implications.
summaries.advanced: Mouse laminar-origin analyses were skipped because whole-cortex laminar data were unavailable. Mouse cytoarchitecture was an ordinal Nissl-based scale (agranular to eulaminate), not a continuous neuron-density map. “Blueprint” is a synthesis of existing tracer resources, not new injections. Core displacement in cat and macaque is reported as an observation with hypothesized vulnerability costs. Catalog organism is mouse; cat, marmoset, and macaque are equally central.

plain_language_summary: Four mammals’ cortical wiring diagrams are compared to see what is shared and what is species-specific. Cell-type architecture, not just distance, helps predict which areas connect, and the most central hubs sit in different kinds of cortex in different species.

ocar.opportunity: A cellular-resolution in vivo atlas of the larval zebrafish brain would give a ground-truth wiring sketch for later synapse-scale EM and a way to map function onto identified morphologies.
ocar.challenge: Without a shared coordinate frame of reconstructed neurons, transgene patterns, and regions, brain-wide dynamics cannot be assigned to circuit architecture.
ocar.action: Kunst, Laurell, Mokayes, Kramer, Baier and colleagues, in Neuron (2019), reconstruct over 2,000 individually GFP-labeled neurons at 6 days post-fertilization, cluster them into morphotypes, co-register over 100 transgene patterns, and annotate 72 non-overlapping brain regions.
ocar.resolution: They generate an inter-areal wiring diagram, demonstrate virtual tract tracing that reveals previously unknown tectal and cerebellar wiring principles, and present the resource as an evolving visualization tool for structure–function mapping in a vertebrate brain.
ocar.future_work: The atlas is described as evolving; synapse-scale EM is positioned as a later use of this light-level ground truth rather than a result of this paper.

summaries.beginner: This atlas traces more than two thousand individually labeled neurons in a baby zebrafish brain and parks them in a shared 3D map. Researchers can look up cell shapes, genetic labels, and which brain regions talk to which.
summaries.intermediate: Published in Neuron (2019), Kunst, Baier and colleagues build an interactive cellular-resolution atlas of the 6 dpf zebrafish brain from reconstructions of over 2,000 individually GFP-labeled neurons, clustered into morphotypes with in vivo coordinates. More than 100 transgene expression patterns were imaged separately and co-registered. Annotating 72 non-overlapping regions yielded an inter-areal wiring diagram intended as ground truth for later EM. Virtual tract tracing is reported to reveal previously unknown wiring principles in tectum and cerebellum.
summaries.advanced: The attached PDF extract is a different paper (Liu, Loring, Naumann, Ijspeert et al., Science Robotics 2025, simZFish/ZBot embodied visuomotor circuits); this annotation follows the catalog abstract only. Neuron count (>2,000), transgene count (>100), and 72 regions are abstract figures. Catalog organism lists fly and zebrafish; the paper is zebrafish. Method metadata lists electron microscopy, but the atlas as described is light-level reconstructions plus registration.

plain_language_summary: This atlas traces more than two thousand individually labeled neurons in a baby zebrafish brain and parks them in a shared 3D map. Researchers can look up cell shapes, genetic labels, and which brain regions talk to which.

ocar.opportunity: All larval Drosophila body-wall motor neurons are identified, so a complete proprioceptor–premotor–motor connectome could show how the same motor pool makes distinct behaviors.
ocar.challenge: Most motor neurons’ roles in locomotion were untested, most premotor neurons unidentified, and proprioceptor–PMN–MN wiring incomplete, leaving open how forward versus backward crawls are generated.
ocar.action: Zarin, Mark, Cardona, Litwin-Kumar, and Doe, on bioRxiv (2019), report that connectome, calcium-imaged muscle/MN phase relationships in forward and backward locomotion, selected motif tests, a candidate escape circuit, and a recurrent network model of the premotor pool.
ocar.resolution: They identify PMN–MN motifs that can produce observed phase relationships, proprioceptor–PMN wiring that anatomically explains proprioception’s effect on locomotor speed, and a model in which the identified premotor neurons suffice for two distinct larval behaviors via behavior-specific motor rhythms.
ocar.future_work: The conclusion is that different locomotor behaviors can arise from a specific premotor group generating behavior-specific rhythms; broader experimental coverage of remaining MNs and behaviors (self-righting, escape) is the implied extension.

summaries.beginner: A crawling fly maggot uses the same motor neurons to walk forward or backward. This team maps the cells that drive those motor neurons and shows, with a model, that one premotor pool can produce both marching orders.
summaries.intermediate: Posted on bioRxiv (2019), Zarin, Mark, Cardona, Litwin-Kumar, and Doe assemble a comprehensive larval proprioceptor–premotor–motor neuron connectome and measure muscle/MN phase during forward and backward crawling. They describe PMN–MN connectivity motifs that could generate those phases (with selected experimental validation), proprioceptor–PMN connections proposed to explain proprioception’s role in locomotor velocity, and a candidate escape motor circuit. A recurrent network model of the identified premotor pool produces the observed motor sequence for two behaviors. The claim is that behavior-specific rhythms from a shared premotor group, not wholly separate motor pools, can generate distinct locomotor patterns.
summaries.advanced: The selected extract’s later pages are blank figure-sheet remnants; quantitative synapse weights, neuron counts, and validation n are not in the usable text. The recurrent model shows sufficiency of the identified PMN pool in silico, not uniqueness. Catalog organism is fly; method is ssTEM connectomics plus calcium imaging and modeling. Preprint, not a later journal version.

plain_language_summary: A crawling fly maggot uses the same motor neurons to walk forward or backward. This team maps the cells that drive those motor neurons and shows, with a model, that one premotor pool can produce both marching orders.

ocar.opportunity: A neuron-to-neuron network built from tens of thousands of single-cell fluorescence reconstructions could reveal community structure of the Drosophila brain without waiting for a complete EM connectome.
ocar.challenge: Without a brain-wide neural network map, systems-level function is hard to study; light-level reconstructions give proximity, not synapses, so communities must be interpreted cautiously.
ocar.action: Shih, Lin, Wang, Lo, Chiang and colleagues, in Neuroinformatics (2019), build a neuron-to-neuron network from 28,573 FlyCircuit v1.2 single-neuron images and run modularity and centrality analyses.
ocar.resolution: They identify eight communities (right/left olfaction, olfactory core, auditory, motor, pre-motor, left/right vision). Different functions dominate different centrality types; overall small-worldness holds except for the two olfactory and the motor communities. A rich club is present, with innermost members mostly innervating the central complex. Numerous loops shorter than seven neurons are reported.
ocar.future_work: The authors treat short loops and function–structure correlations as distinctive processing features; EM validation of light-level edges is the natural caveat for later work.

summaries.beginner: Thousands of individually imaged fly neurons are turned into a brain-wide network sketch. The sketch splits into smell, vision, hearing, and motor neighborhoods, with a tightly linked club of cells in the central complex.
summaries.intermediate: Published in Neuroinformatics (2019), Shih, Lo, Chiang and colleagues construct a neuron-to-neuron network from 28,573 fluorescence images in FlyCircuit v1.2. Modularity analysis yields eight communities: right and left olfaction, olfactory core, auditory, motor, pre-motor, and left and right vision. Centrality analyses suggest function-specific structural roles. Small-worldness is reported for the network except the two olfactory and the motor communities. A rich club is described whose innermost members mostly innervate the central complex, and many loops of length less than seven neurons are identified.
summaries.advanced: The attached PDF extract is a different paper (Liu, White, and Lo, iScience 2025, mutual inhibition and CRIREL motifs); this annotation follows the catalog abstract only. Community names and the 28,573-image count are from the catalog abstract. Light-level FlyCircuit edges are not synaptic EM. Catalog stages include infrastructure and graph_analysis.

plain_language_summary: Thousands of individually imaged fly neurons are turned into a brain-wide network sketch. The sketch splits into smell, vision, hearing, and motor neighborhoods, with a tightly linked club of cells in the central complex.

ocar.opportunity: Fully genetic, multiplexed EM gene reporters would label cell identity without chemical precipitation or antibodies that compromise ultrastructure and tissue penetration.
ocar.challenge: Ferritin’s iron core is small and hard to tell from cellular texture, and existing semi-genetic EM tags need exogenous substrates and permeabilization.
ocar.action: Sigmund, Pettinger, Dietz, Westmeyer and colleagues, on bioRxiv (2019), express the Quasibacillus thermotolerans encapsulin (QtEnc) with native ferroxidase cargo QtlMEF in mammalian cells, compare it to Myxococcus xanthus encapsulin (~32 nm), and train a deep-learning classifier on TEM images.
ocar.resolution: Cryo-EM reconstructions show QtEnc as ~44 nm T=4 icosahedral shells with putative pores at five- and threefold axes; cargo auto-targets the inner surface and sequesters iron efficiently. QtEnc is robustly distinguished from non-intermixing MxEnc, enabling automated multiplexed EM reporter imaging in mammalian cells.
ocar.future_work: Farnesylated Qt variants targeting plasma membrane illustrate spatial addressing; broader in-tissue multiplexing and in vivo use are the implied next tests.

summaries.beginner: Fluorescent proteins come in many colors, but electron microscopy has had few genetic labels that can be told apart. This team grows two sizes of iron-filled protein cages in cells so a computer can read out two gene reporters on ordinary EM pictures.
summaries.intermediate: Posted on bioRxiv (2019), Sigmund, Westmeyer and colleagues introduce Qt encapsulin as a fully genetic iron-biomineralizing EM reporter. QtEnc self-assembles into ~44 nm T=4 nanospheres; native cargo QtlMEF auto-targets the interior and shows ferroxidase activity, sequestering iron in mammalian cells (HEK293T, with Zip14 iron transporter and FAS supplementation in the figures). Mx encapsulin (~32 nm, T=3) does not intermix and is separable by a deep-learning classifier (confusion matrix from 5-fold cross-validation on full-frame TEM). Manual diameter histograms of 100 nanospheres per type support the size split.
summaries.advanced: Classification performance is shown as a confusion matrix in the extract, without a single accuracy number quoted in the selected text. Iron-loading statistics use 3 biological replicates and two-way ANOVA with p < 0.05 post hoc (Supp. Table 3, not excerpted as numbers). This is a methods preprint in cultured cells, not a connectomic reconstruction. Catalog method is TEM; stages include preparation and acquisition.

plain_language_summary: Fluorescent proteins come in many colors, but electron microscopy has had few genetic labels that can be told apart. This team grows two sizes of iron-filled protein cages in cells so a computer can read out two gene reporters on ordinary EM pictures.

ocar.opportunity: Transparent Platynereis larvae allow whole-body cell-type and circuit analysis, including biology absent from C. elegans and Drosophila such as ciliary locomotion, noradrenergic neurons, and ciliary photoreceptors.
ocar.challenge: Neuronal diversity in this annelid must be defined with aligned gene-expression, single-cell RNA-seq, and serial-EM connectomics, plus functional tests, rather than with a single modality.
ocar.action: Williams and Jékely, in Current Opinion in Neurobiology (2019), review neuronal cell types in Platynereis dumerilii identified via whole-body gene-expression atlases, scRNA-seq, serial EM reconstruction, and experimental circuit analysis.
ocar.resolution: They summarize a growing catalog of cell types and circuits and emphasize features that major invertebrate models lack, positioning the larva as a laboratory model for developmental biology and neuroscience.
ocar.future_work: The review points to further functional analysis of identified types and circuits as the path from atlas to mechanism.

summaries.beginner: A small marine worm’s larva is clear enough that researchers can list its neuron types across the whole body. This review surveys those cell types and notes features, such as swimming with cilia, that fruit flies and roundworms do not have.
summaries.intermediate: In Current Opinion in Neurobiology (2019), Williams and Jékely review neuronal cell types in Platynereis dumerilii. Identification methods include whole-body gene-expression atlases, single-cell RNA-seq, and whole-body connectomics from serial EM, with experimental functional analysis of some types and circuits. They highlight biology missing from C. elegans and Drosophila: ciliary locomotion, noradrenergic neurons, and ciliary photoreceptor cells. The larva’s small transparent body is presented as enabling whole-animal cell-type and circuit work.
summaries.advanced: The attached PDF extract is a different paper (Poon, Jékely, and Wan, Science Advances 2025, metachronal waves in the Platynereis ciliary band); this annotation follows the catalog abstract only. No cell-type counts from the CONB review appear in the usable source. Catalog organisms include elegans and other; the paper is an annelid review.

plain_language_summary: A small marine worm’s larva is clear enough that researchers can list its neuron types across the whole body. This review surveys those cell types and notes features, such as swimming with cilia, that fruit flies and roundworms do not have.

ocar.opportunity: The real C. elegans connectome, including extrasynaptic “wireless” aminergic links, lets synchronization and chimera-like states be studied on biological multilayer topology rather than on designed two-layer cartoons.
ocar.challenge: Prior chimera-like states used a constructed split between electrical intra-community and chemical inter-community links; actual electrical, chemical, and extrasynaptic layers may not support the same patterns.
ocar.action: Pournaki, Merfort, Ruiz, Kouvaris, Hövel, and Hizanidis, in Frontiers in Applied Mathematics and Statistics (2019), detect Multilayer-Louvain modules on the three-layer worm network and simulate coupled Hindmarsh–Rose neurons, scoring pairwise Euclidean distances locally and globally.
ocar.resolution: Stronger wireless coupling decreases average coherence locally and globally and does not favor chimera-like states. An alternative partition from dynamical correlations, dominated by two large communities, does promote chimera-like states and maps onto motor-related neurons.
ocar.future_work: They note their correlation-based community algorithm is only one option and invite further topology–dynamics exploration; γthr = 0.30 is a chosen compromise between local synchrony and number of partitions.

summaries.beginner: This theory paper puts living worm wiring, including chemical “wireless” extrasynaptic links, into a simulation of oscillating neurons. Stronger wireless coupling makes the network less synchronized, while a different grouping of cells can produce split, chimera-like rhythms tied to motor neurons.
summaries.intermediate: Published in Frontiers in Applied Mathematics and Statistics (2019), Pournaki and colleagues study synchronization on a three-layer C. elegans connectome (electrical synapses, chemical synapses, extrasynaptic wireless). Multilayer-Louvain communities define modules; Hindmarsh–Rose oscillators are coupled on that topology. Wireless coupling tends to reduce local and global coherence and does not favor chimera-like states. Re-clustering by dynamical correlations yields a structure dominated by two large communities that does support chimera-like states and relates corresponding neurons to motor functions. Parameter scans include gel, gch, and gwl; one reported search kept 582 of 5250 partitions at γthr = 0.30.
summaries.advanced: Chimera-like states depend on how communities are defined; the biologically layered Louvain partition and the correlation-based partition disagree on whether they appear. Hindmarsh–Rose dynamics are a modeling choice, not recorded membrane potentials. Wireless layer strength is a parameter sweep, not a measured extrasynaptic conductance. Catalog organism is elegans; this is computational neuroscience on published connectivity, not new EM.

plain_language_summary: This theory paper puts living worm wiring, including chemical “wireless” extrasynaptic links, into a simulation of oscillating neurons. Stronger wireless coupling makes the network less synchronized, while a different grouping of cells can produce split, chimera-like rhythms tied to motor neurons.

ocar.opportunity: Fruit-fly heading neurons form a ring attractor; locusts have a homologous central-complex circuit with different projection and connectivity details, so modeling both can show how architecture tunes compass dynamics.
ocar.challenge: It was unclear whether the locust motif still supports a ring attractor and how structural differences trade speed of heading updates against noise tolerance.
ocar.action: Pisokas, Heinze, and Webb, on bioRxiv (2019), model the precise connectivity patterns of Drosophila and locust central-complex heading circuits and compare their dynamics.
ocar.resolution: The locust circuit can operate as a ring attractor. Differences enable the fruit-fly circuit to respond faster to heading changes while making the locust circuit more tolerant to noise. Subtle projection-pattern differences therefore change circuit performance.
ocar.future_work: The authors emphasize a comparative neuroscience need: homologous architecture is not identical function, so connectivity details should be modeled species by species.

summaries.beginner: Flies and locusts both have a brain compass built from a ring of cells, but the wiring is not identical. This modeling study finds the locust version can still hold a heading, while the fly version updates faster and the locust version shrugs off noise better.
summaries.intermediate: Posted on bioRxiv (2019), Pisokas, Heinze, and Webb compare head-direction ring-attractor circuits in Drosophila melanogaster and locusts, using species-specific central-complex projection patterns. Both are treated as homologous topographic circuits with significant structural and connectivity differences. Simulations show the locust circuit can function as a ring attractor. Parameter exploration of connectivity indicates the fly circuit responds faster to heading changes, whereas the locust circuit is more noise-tolerant. The discussion frames this as evidence that small projection differences matter and that comparative modeling is required.
summaries.advanced: The selected extract’s later pages are references; quantitative speed or noise-tolerance values are not in the usable text. This is a computational study of published neuroanatomy, not new physiology. Catalog organism is fly; locust is an equal focus. Preprint, not a later eLife/journal version.

plain_language_summary: Flies and locusts both have a brain compass built from a ring of cells, but the wiring is not identical. This modeling study finds the locust version can still hold a heading, while the fly version updates faster and the locust version shrugs off noise better.

ocar.opportunity: Connectomes are growing faster than reconstruction teams can analyze them, so tools, archives, and downstream simulators must be planned before analysis becomes the bottleneck.
ocar.challenge: Unlike genomics, connectomics lacks standardized analyses, file formats, and a funded long-term archive; each group uses ad hoc Matlab, R, Python, or C++ against nonstandard files or queries.
ocar.action: Scheffer, in Frontiers in Neural Circuits (2018), classifies analyses into interactive reconstruction aids, publication-grade reproducible scripts, and import into simulation or machine learning, and he discusses synapse inclusion, transmitters, and reduction of detail.
ocar.resolution: Near-term he recommends publishing analysis code and data interfaces; long-term he expects an NCBI-like facility. Downstream use requires intelligent reduction of huge reconstructions and merging of genetic and optical data the EM volume lacks.
ocar.future_work: He predicts that as circuit motifs become clearer, a standard analysis suite may emerge, as in genomics, and that analysis teams will often be distinct from reconstruction teams.

summaries.beginner: Wiring diagrams of brains are getting so large that analyzing them is becoming harder than collecting them. This essay sorts the needed software into tools for tracing, tools for papers, and tools for simulations, and it argues for a shared public archive.
summaries.intermediate: Published in Frontiers in Neural Circuits (2018), Scheffer reviews analysis tools for large connectomes. He distinguishes (1) interactive tools used during reconstruction, (2) analyses supporting papers that must be archived and reproducible, and (3) import into neural simulation or machine learning. He notes that connectomic analyses are still dataset-specific, with no standard file format or funded archive, and he recommends publishing code plus the data interface. Downstream modeling requires choosing which synapses to keep (recall–precision), assigning transmitters from separate databases, and coupling to mechanics and sensors. He analogizes a future central query facility to NCBI.
summaries.advanced: This is an opinion/review from a reconstruction practitioner, not a new software release with benchmarks. No dataset sizes or error rates are quantified in the extract. Catalog role is history; the piece is prospective infrastructure. Claims about genomics’ rapid split between data producers and analysts are analogical.

plain_language_summary: Wiring diagrams of brains are getting so large that analyzing them is becoming harder than collecting them. This essay sorts the needed software into tools for tracing, tools for papers, and tools for simulations, and it argues for a shared public archive.

ocar.opportunity: Network control theory can turn a C. elegans wiring diagram plus muscles into predictions about which neurons must be driven to produce behavior, uniting structure and function in one mathematical language.
ocar.challenge: Naive driver-node searches on the whole nervous system are hard to interpret biologically; some ablation phenotypes are missed, and weights, signs, nonlinearity, and proprioception are still largely absent.
ocar.action: Towlson, Vértes, Yan, Chew, Walker, Schafer, and Barabási, in Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society B (2018), review their 2017 Nature control analysis as an FAQ and release Python code for worm-specific control experiments.
ocar.resolution: Formulating target control with muscles as outputs yielded successful, sometimes non-obvious predictions (e.g. PDB affecting ventral bias of omega turns despite few synapses; posterior DD neurons weighted over anterior). Neurons flagged for controllability are likely to affect real behavior, even if the reverse—every ablation phenotype—is not recovered.
ocar.future_work: They expect calcium imaging to supply weights and signs for control energy and time, and they warn that higher animals will need explicit problem statements (e.g. steering a region away from seizure) plus nonlinearity and feedback.

summaries.beginner: This FAQ explains a math framework that asks which worm neurons you must “drive” to control crawling muscles. Some predicted cells were surprising, such as a tail neuron that affects how the animal turns.
summaries.intermediate: In Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society B (2018), Towlson and colleagues review network control as applied to C. elegans (Yan et al. 2017 Nature) in FAQ form, covering theory, computation, experiment, limits, and Python code. Target control with muscles as output nodes produced interpretable predictions, unlike searching for driver nodes among all neurons. Recovered examples include PDB (similar omega-turn ventral-bias phenotype to RIV despite few synapses) and a predicted greater importance of individual dorsal DD neurons than anterior ones. Missed ablation phenotypes (e.g. SMB, RIV in some implementations) are acknowledged. The article sits in a ‘Connectome to behaviour’ discussion issue.
summaries.advanced: This is a review/FAQ of a prior Nature paper, not a new connectome. Success is framed as: identified controllability neurons likely affect behavior, not that all behavioral neurons are found. Code is provided for this organism specifically. Catalog role is history/infrastructure. Functional weights and signs remain future data needs, as stated.

plain_language_summary: This FAQ explains a math framework that asks which worm neurons you must “drive” to control crawling muscles. Some predicted cells were surprising, such as a tail neuron that affects how the animal turns.

ocar.opportunity: The zebrafish lateral-line neuromast is a small, stereotyped hair-cell circuit that can be fully wired in multiple animals, stages, and genotypes to study how microcircuits assemble.
ocar.challenge: Axons still face many possible hair-cell partners; activity, planar polarity, and Notch-dependent sibling identity could all explain directional wiring, and they are confounded without complete contact maps.
ocar.action: Dow, Jacobo, Hossain, Siletti, and Hudspeth, in eLife (2018), use serial block-face SEM on multiple specimens to reconstruct the neuromast connectome of hair cells with afferent and efferent fibers, and they compare vangl2 mutants and Notch-overexpressing larvae.
ocar.resolution: Each afferent terminal receives hair cells of one directional sensitivity; innervation is redundant; terminals show a dominance hierarchy. vangl2 (trilobite) randomizes sibling position and bundle orientation but wiring specificity remains; Notch overexpression yields uniformly oriented, uniformly innervating siblings, so specificity is attributed to Notch signaling. Average hair cells form ribbon synapses with two or more afferents, membrane contacts with four, and sit near five or more afferents perisynaptically; one efferent per neuromast contacts every mature hair cell of both polarities.
ocar.future_work: They conclude coincident depolarization is neither necessary nor sufficient for specificity and that each daughter hair cell acquires a biochemical identity guiding innervation; how Notch assigns that identity molecularly is the open mechanistic step.

summaries.beginner: In a baby zebrafish’s lateral line, hair cells that point different ways plug into different nerve endings with striking precision. Mutants that scramble cell orientation still wire specifically, pointing to a molecular identity signal rather than to cells simply firing together.
summaries.intermediate: Published in eLife (2018; catalog lists bioRxiv), Dow, Hudspeth and colleagues reconstruct neuromast connectomes with SBSEM across multiple specimens. Wiring shows directional specificity, redundancy, and hierarchical dominance of afferent terminals. In vangl2/trilobite mutants, sibling hair cells are randomly placed and oriented yet retain specific innervation; Notch-overexpressing larvae have uniformly oriented siblings that innervate uniformly, implicating Notch. Developmental increase in contact specificity is reported. One efferent axon per neuromast contacts every mature hair cell. Video reconstructions illustrate a trilobite neuromast with eight hair cells and eleven axonal terminals (specimen T1).
summaries.advanced: T1 video numbers (8 hair cells, 11 terminals) are for one mutant specimen, not the wild-type mean. Ribbon-synapse “two or more,” membrane contacts “four,” and perisynaptic “five or more” are stated averages in the discussion. Fracture of hair-bundle tips in T1 required confocal polarity assignment. Catalog journal is bioRxiv; the extract is the eLife paper. Catalog method is SEM; the technique is serial block-face SEM.

plain_language_summary: In a baby zebrafish’s lateral line, hair cells that point different ways plug into different nerve endings with striking precision. Mutants that scramble cell orientation still wire specifically, pointing to a molecular identity signal rather than to cells simply firing together.

ocar.opportunity: If neuron morphology and regional white-matter degree covary in multiple mammals, micro–macro coupling would be a conserved feature of cortical architecture, not a human MRI artifact.
ocar.challenge: Prior cat, macaque, and human reports needed replication in additional species and with mixed reconstruction methods (tracers versus diffusion MRI).
ocar.action: Scholtens, Barrett, and van den Heuvel, in Brain Connectivity (2018), combine NeuroMorpho.org reconstructions with tract-tracing connectomes (rat, mouse) and in vivo dMRI (human) and correlate regional morphology with macroscale projection counts.
ocar.resolution: Across human, mouse, and rat, cortical variation in neuronal complexity, including soma surface, explains significant proportions of variation in white-matter projection numbers (human soma surface vs connectivity over 10 regions; rat and mouse soma surface vs out-degree). PCA on microscale features yielded two components per dataset (>95% variance), and effects were tested at a partial Bonferroni alpha of 0.025.
ocar.future_work: They present the association as a central aspect of mammalian neural architecture, consistent with cytoarchitectonic prediction of pathways in other species; causal direction (morphology shaping projections versus the reverse) is not resolved here.

summaries.beginner: In humans, mice, and rats, brain areas whose neurons are larger or more complex also tend to send more long-range cables. This paper treats that micro-to-macro match as a shared design feature of mammalian cortex.
summaries.intermediate: Published in Brain Connectivity (2018), Scholtens, Barrett, and van den Heuvel test whether regional neuron morphology from NeuroMorpho.org covaries with macroscale connectivity in human (dMRI), mouse (tract tracing), and rat (tract tracing). Cross-scale plots highlight soma surface versus connectivity (human, 10 cortical regions with NeuroMorpho data) and soma surface versus out-degree (rat, mouse). PCA indicated two microscale components explaining >95% of variance in each dataset; significance used partial Bonferroni alpha 0.05/2 = 0.025. Findings are presented as converging with cat/macaque/human reports that larger, more complex pyramids have more corticocortical connections.
summaries.advanced: Human n is 10 regions with available reconstructions, not whole-cortex coverage. Connectivity modalities differ (dMRI vs tracers), so cross-species correlation strength should not be pooled as one number—the extract does not quote r values in the selected text. Catalog organism is mouse; human and rat are co-equal. This is collated analysis, not new tracing or new neuron fills.

plain_language_summary: In humans, mice, and rats, brain areas whose neurons are larger or more complex also tend to send more long-range cables. This paper treats that micro-to-macro match as a shared design feature of mammalian cortex.

ocar.opportunity: Neuroscience applications repeatedly rebuild the same visualization, data-source, and simulation-control infrastructure; a shared middleware could let groups write only domain-specific code.
ocar.challenge: Independent tools for NeuroML models, fly anatomy, NEURON, and NetPyNE look unrelated, yet they share needs to load models, plot activity, and talk to simulators.
ocar.action: Cantarelli, Marin, Quintana, Earnshaw, Court, Gleeson, Dura-Bernal, Silver, and Idili, in Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society B (2018), present Geppetto, an open-source frontend/backend platform with domain-agnostic model abstractions.
ocar.resolution: Geppetto underpins Open Source Brain, Virtual Fly Brain, NEURON-UI, and NetPyNE-UI, and is also used in Patient H.M., WormSim, and SciDash. OSB visualizes and simulates NeuroML in the browser; VFB hosts Drosophila neuropil, neurons, stacks, and expression data.
ocar.future_work: They argue reuse of modules beats monoliths; success is measured by further applications skipping common infrastructure rather than by a single new scientific result.

summaries.beginner: Many neuroscience websites need the same 3D viewers and simulation knobs. Geppetto is shared plumbing so fly atlases, worm simulations, and NEURON interfaces do not each rebuild those pieces from scratch.
summaries.intermediate: Published in Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society B (2018), Cantarelli and colleagues describe Geppetto as reusable middleware for visualizing neuroscience models and data and managing simulations. Applications include Open Source Brain (NeuroML models in-browser), Virtual Fly Brain (Drosophila anatomy and imaging), NEURON-UI, and NetPyNE-UI, plus Patient H.M., WormSim, and SciDash. A backend connects to external data sources, model repositories, and simulators; a customizable frontend supplies widgets. Domain-agnostic abstractions are meant to represent diverse models. The article is part of a C. elegans cellular-resolution modelling discussion issue.
summaries.advanced: This is a software-platform paper; no connectome accuracy metrics appear. Overlap among independently specified applications is the authors’ justification for middleware, not a controlled reuse study. Catalog organism is elegans (WormSim/OpenWorm context) though VFB is Drosophila. Catalog stages include segmentation, which Geppetto does not perform; it visualizes and simulates existing models and data.

plain_language_summary: Many neuroscience websites need the same 3D viewers and simulation knobs. Geppetto is shared plumbing so fly atlases, worm simulations, and NEURON interfaces do not each rebuild those pieces from scratch.
